headings.title: Understanding Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder in the Nigerian Context
headings.content: Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder, commonly known as **OCD**, is a chronic mental health condition marked by intrusive thoughts and repetitive behaviors. In Nigerian communities, psychiatric symptoms are frequently interpreted through a religious or cultural lens. A woman experiencing severe intrusive thoughts about harming her baby may fear she has been cursed, or that evil spiritual forces are attacking her mind. Midwives must recognize that while spiritual beliefs provide vital comfort to many patients, clinical conditions like OCD require medical understanding alongside spiritual support. Recognizing OCD prevents harmful delays in seeking proper care and protects mothers from unnecessary social isolation.

headings.title: The Core Components: Obsessions Versus Compulsions
headings.content:
- **Obsessions**: These are recurring, unwanted thoughts, mental images, or urges that trigger intense anxiety or distress. Common examples include a persistent fear of contamination or distressing thoughts of accidentally dropping a newborn.
- **Compulsions**: These are repetitive physical acts or mental rituals that a person feels driven to perform in response to an obsession. Typical behaviors involve excessive handwashing, repeatedly checking door locks, or counting objects in a specific sequence.

While obsessions cause extreme anxiety, compulsions serve as a temporary attempt to neutralize that anxiety. Unfortunately, performing the ritual only reinforces the cycle, making the obsession return with greater force over time.

headings.title: Clinical Presentation and Common Symptom Themes in Midwifery Practice
headings.content: Pregnant and postpartum women face unique vulnerabilities that can trigger or worsen OCD symptoms. Hormonal fluctuations, sleep deprivation, and the immense responsibility of caring for a newborn create fertile ground for anxiety disorders. Common themes observed in maternity wards include contamination fears involving hospital germs, excessive cleaning of infant feeding equipment, and terrifying intrusive thoughts of harming the baby. Unlike mothers with postpartum psychosis, women with OCD find these violent thoughts deeply horrifying and are intensely afraid of acting on them. They actively avoid knives, stairs, or holding the baby alone when anxiety peaks, yet they remain fully in touch with reality.

headings.title: Pathophysiology and Contributing Psychological Factors
headings.content: The exact biological origins of OCD involve complex interactions within the central nervous system. Neuroimaging studies suggest abnormalities in frontal-subcortical circuits, which regulate filtering of thoughts and motor behaviors. Neurotransmitter imbalances, particularly involving **serotonin**, play a major role in sustaining these neural loops. Psychological stressors, including a history of trauma, extreme life changes, or a perfectionist personality style, can also precipitate the onset of symptoms during the vulnerable childbearing years.

headings.title: Screening and Identifying OCD in Pregnant and Postpartum Women
headings.content: Routine antenatal and postnatal visits offer ideal opportunities to screen for mental health challenges. Many mothers hide their compulsions out of shame, fearing healthcare workers will report them to child welfare services as unfit parents. Midwives must ask gentle, normalizing questions about worries and mental routines. Using validated screening tools, alongside empathetic listening, helps uncover hidden suffering. A pregnant woman who spends hours checking her antenatal records or washing her hands raw deserves patient-centered inquiry rather than dismissal.

headings.title: Holistic Management and Nursing Care Strategies
headings.content: Managing OCD effectively requires a collaborative approach involving midwives, mental health specialists, and the family. First-line treatments typically combine specialized psychotherapy, such as **Cognitive Behavioral Therapy** with Exposure and Response Prevention, alongside pharmacotherapy when symptoms are severe. Midwives contribute by establishing a safe environment, offering psychoeducation to reduce guilt, and coordinating referrals to psychiatric services. Practical support also includes helping family members understand that compulsions are symptoms of an illness, not deliberate choices.

headings.title: Supporting Maternal Mental Health and Reducing Stigma
headings.content: Stigma remains a massive barrier to mental healthcare across Nigeria. Many individuals view psychiatric disorders as personal weaknesses or spiritual failures, which drives mothers to suffer in silence. Midwives occupy a trusted position in the community and can lead advocacy efforts by normalizing conversations about emotional wellbeing during antenatal classes. By treating mental health with the same urgency as physical complications like hemorrhage or pre-eclampsia, midwives empower women to seek help early, ensuring healthier outcomes for both mother and child.
